patient.name: Sophie Mensah
patient.complaint: Abdominal pain that started around the belly button and has moved to the right lower side
background: Last menstrual period 2 weeks ago; uses condoms
Postgraduate student at a university in Bloomsbury

diagnosis.exam: Expect 'Which is the most likely diagnosis?' with central pain migrating to the RIF, anorexia and fever, or a sign question (Rovsing's, psoas, obturator) where the sign tells you the appendix position.

points: Sophie, 23, woke yesterday with a dull ache **around her umbilicus**.
Overnight it moved and sharpened in the **right iliac fossa**.
Off her food since yesterday; vomited twice.
The car journey in was agony over every bump.

visual.title: Where Sophie's pain went
visual.caption: Central, poorly localised pain first, then sharp pain fixed in the right iliac fossa.

steps.text: This migration is the single most useful clue in the history.

steps.lead: Sophie's appendix lumen is probably blocked, most often by a **faecolith** in adults.
Sophie has the full picture: **migratory pain**, anorexia, vomiting, fever and pain on moving.

points: Maximal tenderness at **McBurney's point** with guarding.
Pressing her **left** iliac fossa makes the **right** side hurt.
Rebound tenderness; coughing makes her wince.
No vaginal discharge; no urinary symptoms.

steps.q: Pressing Sophie's LIF causes pain in her RIF. What is this sign?
steps.r: **Rovsing's sign**: RIF pain on palpating the LIF. Murphy's is RUQ (gallbladder).

steps.lead: Sophie's psoas and obturator signs are negative, so her appendix probably sits in the usual position, not retrocaecal or pelvic.

steps.title: Right iliac fossa pain in a young woman
head: Feature
Appendicitis
Ectopic pregnancy
Mesenteric adenitis

steps.lead: Sophie presented in 24 hours. Left for days, she could form an **appendix mass** or **abscess** with a swinging fever.

steps.text: Do not let a young woman with RIF pain go to theatre without a **pregnancy test**. A ruptured ectopic is the killer differential.

investigation.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?' in a young woman (pregnancy test), or imaging choice: ultrasound in children, pregnancy and young women; CT in adults when unclear.

steps.q: Which test must Sophie have first?
steps.r: Every woman of childbearing age with abdominal pain needs a **beta-hCG** to exclude ectopic pregnancy.

steps.lead: Sophie's **beta-hCG is negative** and her **urine dip** shows no nitrites or leucocytes, so ectopic and UTI are unlikely.

steps.title: Sophie's bloods
steps.text: Raised inflammatory markers support the diagnosis but cannot prove it.

steps.lead: Sophie is a young woman with a clear picture, so **ultrasound** comes first. **CT** is the adult choice if USS is equivocal or she deteriorates.

visual.title: Appendix diameter on ultrasound
visual.label: Sophie 10 mm
visual.caption: A non-compressible appendix over 6 mm with surrounding fluid supports appendicitis.

steps.title: Imaging choice
nodes: Child, pregnant or young woman → ultrasound
Other adults, unclear or equivocal USS → CT with contrast
steps.caption: Imaging supports the clinical diagnosis; histology proves it.

steps.lead: Sophie's diagnosis is still clinical; the **histology** of her removed appendix will confirm it.

steps.text: A **normal appendix with enlarged mesenteric nodes** on imaging after a viral illness is mesenteric adenitis, managed supportively.

management.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate definitive management?' (laparoscopic appendicectomy), or a twist: appendix mass (antibiotics, drainage, interval surgery) or perforation with peritonitis (urgent surgery).

steps.lead: Sophie is made **nil by mouth**, given IV fluids, analgesia, an anti-emetic and **prophylactic IV antibiotics** before theatre.

steps.q: Which is the definitive treatment for Sophie?
steps.r: Early **laparoscopic appendicectomy** is definitive. Antibiotics alone are only for select uncomplicated cases.

steps.lead: Sophie has a laparoscopic appendicectomy that evening with **amoxicillin, gentamicin and metronidazole** around the operation.

steps.title: Which path?
nodes: Peritonitis or sepsis → perforation: urgent surgery
Appendix mass or abscess → IV antibiotics and drainage
Mass not settled by 6 weeks → interval appendicectomy
steps.caption: The examination and imaging decide which branch.

steps.lead: If Sophie's pain had spread and become rigid with sepsis, that means **perforation** and she would go to theatre urgently.
Had Sophie presented after a week with a tender RIF mass, she would have IV antibiotics, drainage and **delayed surgery** instead.

visual.title: Sophie after appendicectomy
visual.caption: CRP peaks the day after surgery then falls. A swinging fever after day 3 would suggest an abscess.

steps.text: Sudden **relief** of RIF pain followed by worse generalised pain is not improvement: it suggests the appendix has **perforated**.

science.exam: Expect applied questions: why the pain starts centrally (midgut visceral pain) and moves to the RIF (parietal peritoneum), or what a sign says about the appendix position.

steps.lead: Sophie's faecolith raised the pressure in her appendix: **veins** close first, then arteries, so the wall becomes ischaemic and infected.

steps.title: From blockage to perforation
nodes: Faecolith or lymphoid hyperplasia blocks the lumen
Mucus builds up: intraluminal pressure rises
Venous drainage fails, then arterial supply

steps.q: Why did Sophie's pain start around her umbilicus?
o: Visceral pain referred via midgut autonomic nerves
steps.r: The appendix is a **midgut** structure, so distension gives vague **visceral** pain referred to the periumbilical area (T10).

steps.lead: Overnight the inflammation reached Sophie's **parietal peritoneum**, which has somatic nerves, so the pain became sharp and fixed at McBurney's point.
A retrocaecal appendix irritates **psoas** (hip extension hurts); a pelvic one irritates **obturator internus** (internal rotation hurts).
If Sophie's appendix had perforated, her **omentum** might wall it off into an abscess; if not, she would get generalised peritonitis.

steps.text: Children get more **lymphoid hyperplasia** (often after a viral illness) and have a thin omentum, so they perforate and spread infection more readily.

mcq.q: What is the classic pain pattern of appendicitis?
o: Epigastric pain radiating to the back
Periumbilical pain migrating to the RIF
mcq.r: Central visceral pain moving to the **RIF** as the parietal peritoneum becomes inflamed.

o: Pain on internal rotation of the flexed hip
Pain on hyperextension of the right hip
RIF pain on palpation of the LIF
mcq.r: **RIF pain when the LIF is pressed.**

mcq.q: A positive psoas sign suggests which appendix position?
mcq.r: Hip hyperextension stretches psoas against a **retrocaecal** appendix.

mcq.q: Most common cause of luminal obstruction in children?
mcq.r: **Lymphoid hyperplasia** is more common in children; faecolith overall.

mcq.q: First-line imaging for suspected appendicitis in pregnancy?
mcq.r: **Ultrasound** first in children, pregnancy and young women.
Diagnosis is clinical, confirmed by **histology** of the removed appendix.

mcq.q: What is the definitive management of acute appendicitis?
Which perioperative antibiotic combination is commonly used?
mcq.r: IV **amoxicillin, gentamicin and metronidazole** for 24 hours.

mcq.q: Appendix mass not improved after 6 weeks of treatment. Next step?
mcq.r: **Interval appendicectomy** if the mass has not settled by 6 weeks.

mcq.q: Why does the pain move to the RIF?
mcq.r: Somatic pain from the **parietal peritoneum** localises precisely over McBurney's point.

technique.stem: A 17 year old boy has a 20 hour history of abdominal pain that began around his umbilicus and is now in the right iliac fossa. He has no appetite and has vomited once. Pressing on the left iliac fossa causes pain in the right iliac fossa. His temperature is 37.8°C and pulse rate 98 bpm.
technique.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

steps.x: A diagnosis question about RIF pain: the pain pattern and the signs decide it.

clues: began around his umbilicus and is now in the right iliac fossa
Pressing on the left iliac fossa causes pain in the right iliac fossa
steps.x: Migratory pain, anorexia, **Rovsing's sign** and a low-grade fever.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Classic **acute appendicitis**.

elim: Crohn's is a chronic picture with diarrhoea and weight loss.
Adenitis follows a viral illness and lacks localised peritonism.
Ureteric colic is loin to groin, colicky, with haematuria.
Torsion gives sudden testicular pain; always examine the testes, but migration fits the appendix.

steps.x: **A. Acute appendicitis.** Rule: central pain → RIF + anorexia + Rovsing's = appendix.

technique.stem: A 29 year old woman who is 20 weeks pregnant has a 1 day history of central abdominal pain that has moved to the right side. She has vomited twice. She is tender on the right with guarding. Her temperature is 37.9°C, pulse rate 104 bpm and BP 112/70 mmHg.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate initial imaging investigation?
o: CT abdomen and pelvis with contrast

steps.x: Imaging choice: who is the patient?

clues: central abdominal pain that has moved to the right side
steps.x: Suspected appendicitis in **pregnancy**: avoid radiation.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Ultrasound**, first-line in children, pregnancy and young women.

elim: CT gives radiation; used in non-pregnant adults when unclear.
Erect CXR looks for free air in perforation.
AXR does not diagnose appendicitis.
Amylase is a blood test for pancreatitis, not imaging.

steps.x: **E. Ultrasound abdomen.** Rule: child, pregnant or young woman = USS first.

technique.stem: A 34 year old man has had right iliac fossa pain for 2 days. This morning the pain spread across his whole abdomen. He is lying still, his abdomen is rigid with generalised guarding and he has no bowel sounds. His temperature is 38.9°C, pulse rate 124 bpm, BP 94/58 mmHg and respiratory rate 26 breaths per minute.
technique.q: After resuscitation and IV antibiotics, which is the most appropriate management?

steps.x: Management after resuscitation: is this simple, a mass, or perforation?
Generalised peritonitis with sepsis: **perforated appendicitis**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Urgent surgery**: appendicectomy with washout.

elim: Drainage is for a localised abscess, not generalised peritonitis.
Interval surgery is for an appendix mass that has settled.
Antibiotics alone will not control a perforation.
He is septic; oral treatment is unsafe.

steps.x: **B. Emergency appendicectomy.** Rule: peritonitis + sepsis = perforation = urgent surgery.

technique.stem: A 20 year old man has appendicitis caused by a faecolith blocking the appendiceal lumen. Mucus continues to be secreted behind the obstruction and the intraluminal pressure rises.
technique.q: Which is the first vascular consequence of the rising intraluminal pressure?

steps.x: Mechanism: what fails first as pressure rises?
Low-pressure **veins** collapse before high-pressure arteries.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Venous drainage** is impaired first, then arterial supply, then ischaemia.

elim: Arterial supply fails later, from pressure, not primary thrombosis.
Vasospasm is not the mechanism.
Emboli cause mesenteric ischaemia, not appendicitis.
Portal pyaemia is a rare late complication.

steps.x: **C. Impaired venous drainage.** Then arterial supply fails, then necrosis and perforation.

practice.stem: A 21 year old man has a 1 day history of abdominal pain. It began as a dull ache around his umbilicus and is now sharp in the right iliac fossa. He has lost his appetite and the pain is worse when he coughs. His temperature is 37.8°C, pulse rate 100 bpm, BP 124/78 mmHg and respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute.

visual.title: Site of pain
visual.caption: Pain moved from the umbilical region to the right iliac fossa.

practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Migratory central-to-RIF pain with anorexia, fever and pain on coughing is acute appendicitis. Ureteric colic is colicky loin-to-groin pain.

steps.x: Diagnosis of RIF pain in a young man.

clues: dull ache around his umbilicus and is now sharp in the right iliac fossa
steps.x: Migration, anorexia and peritonism.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Acute appendicitis**.

elim: Crohn's gives chronic diarrhoea and weight loss.
Meckel's is rare and usually presents with painless bleeding in children.
Adenitis follows a viral illness, without migration.
Colic radiates loin to groin and comes in waves.

steps.x: **A. Acute appendicitis.**

practice.stem: A 15 year old girl has an 18 hour history of abdominal pain that started centrally and is now in the right iliac fossa. Her pregnancy test is negative. She is tender at McBurney's point. Her temperature is 37.7°C and pulse rate 96 bpm.
practice.q: Which additional sign is most likely to be present on palpation of her left iliac fossa?
practice.e: Rovsing's sign is RIF pain on palpation of the LIF, seen in appendicitis. Murphy's sign is for cholecystitis; Cullen's and Grey Turner's are bruising in haemorrhagic pancreatitis.

steps.x: A finding question: which sign comes from pressing the LIF?

clues: started centrally and is now in the right iliac fossa
steps.x: Appendicitis with ectopic excluded. The question asks which sign pressing the LIF gives.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Rovsing's sign**.

elim: Boas's sign is hyperaesthesia below the right scapula in cholecystitis.
Cullen's is periumbilical bruising in pancreatitis.
Grey Turner's is flank bruising in pancreatitis.
Murphy's is RUQ, for cholecystitis.

steps.x: **E. Rovsing's sign.**

practice.stem: A 26 year old man has a 2 day history of right-sided abdominal and flank pain with anorexia. He walks with his right hip slightly flexed. Abdominal tenderness is mild, but hyperextending his right hip causes severe pain. His temperature is 37.9°C and pulse rate 104 bpm. Urinalysis shows no blood.
practice.q: Which is the most likely position of his inflamed appendix?
practice.e: A positive psoas sign (pain on right hip hyperextension) with mild anterior tenderness suggests a retrocaecal appendix. A pelvic appendix gives a positive obturator sign.

steps.x: Which position? Match the sign to the anatomy.

clues: hyperextending his right hip causes severe pain
steps.x: **Psoas sign**; the appendix lies behind the caecum, away from the anterior wall.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Retrocaecal**.

elim: Paracaecal does not classically irritate psoas.
Pelvic gives the obturator sign and urinary or rectal symptoms.
Pre-ileal gives typical anterior signs.
Subcaecal gives typical anterior RIF tenderness.

steps.x: **D. Retrocaecal.** Psoas = retrocaecal; obturator = pelvic.

practice.stem: A 31 year old woman has had right iliac fossa pain for 6 days. She did not seek help sooner. She now has a tender, palpable mass in the right iliac fossa and a swinging fever. Her pregnancy test is negative. Her temperature is 38.4°C, pulse rate 102 bpm and BP 120/76 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: A late presentation of appendicitis with a palpable RIF mass and swinging fever is an appendix mass. Caecal carcinoma is a slow history in an older patient.

steps.x: Diagnosis: a complication of a common condition presenting late.

clues: tender, palpable mass in the right iliac fossa
steps.x: Late appendicitis walled off into a mass, with an abscess component.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Appendix mass**; ultrasound would show the abscess.

elim: Caecal cancer is gradual, with anaemia, in older patients.
Crohn's can cause a mass but is chronic with diarrhoea.
An uncomplicated cyst does not cause swinging fever.
TOA follows pelvic inflammatory disease with discharge, often bilateral.

steps.x: **A. Appendix mass.** Late appendicitis + RIF mass + swinging fever.

practice.stem: A 40 year old man had right iliac fossa pain for 2 days, which briefly eased this morning. Over the last 4 hours the pain has spread over his whole abdomen. He is lying very still with a rigid abdomen. His temperature is 39.0°C, pulse rate 126 bpm, BP 92/56 mmHg and respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: RIF pain that briefly eased then became generalised peritonitis with sepsis is perforated appendicitis. A peptic perforation starts in the epigastrium.

steps.x: Diagnosis: what happened to the RIF pain?

clues: right iliac fossa pain for 2 days
steps.x: Relief then generalised peritonitis and septic shock.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Perforated appendicitis**.

elim: An abscess is walled off with a localised mass and swinging fever.
Ischaemia gives pain out of proportion to signs, with AF.
Peptic perforation starts epigastric, often after NSAIDs.
Obstruction gives distension, vomiting and absolute constipation.

steps.x: **C. Perforated appendicitis.** Brief relief then worse = rupture.

practice.stem: An 8 year old boy has a 1 day history of central abdominal pain moving to the right iliac fossa, with vomiting. He had a sore throat and runny nose last week. He has RIF tenderness and guarding. His temperature is 38.0°C and pulse rate 118 bpm. Ultrasound shows a dilated, non-compressible appendix.
practice.q: Which is the most likely cause of the luminal obstruction?
practice.e: Lymphoid hyperplasia, often after a viral infection, is the more common cause of luminal obstruction in children. A faecolith is the most common cause overall and in adults.

steps.x: Cause of the obstruction: who is the patient?

clues: sore throat and runny nose last week
steps.x: A child, after a viral illness, with confirmed appendicitis.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Lymphoid hyperplasia**.

elim: Carcinoid is rare, usually found incidentally in adults.
Faecolith is most common in adults; the viral illness points to lymphoid tissue.
Foreign bodies are rare.
Threadworm is a rare cause and gives perianal itch.

steps.x: **D. Lymphoid hyperplasia.** Children + recent viral illness.

practice.stem: A 24 year old woman has a 1 day history of central abdominal pain that has moved to the right iliac fossa, with anorexia. Her last menstrual period was 6 weeks ago. She has RIF tenderness. Her temperature is 37.6°C, pulse rate 98 bpm and BP 116/72 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?
practice.e: Every woman of childbearing age with RIF pain needs a pregnancy test first to exclude ectopic pregnancy. Imaging comes after.

steps.x: Initial investigation in a young woman with RIF pain.

clues: last menstrual period was 6 weeks ago
steps.x: Missed period: ectopic must be excluded before anything else.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Pregnancy test (beta-hCG)**.

elim: AXR does not help diagnose appendicitis.
CT gives radiation and should follow a pregnancy test.
Amylase is for pancreatitis.
TVUS follows a positive beta-hCG.

steps.x: **E. Urine beta-hCG.** Rule: woman + abdominal pain = pregnancy test first.

practice.stem: A 62 year old man has a 3 day history of lower abdominal pain, worse on the right, with anorexia. Examination is equivocal, with mild right-sided tenderness. His temperature is 37.8°C, pulse rate 96 bpm and BP 138/84 mmHg. An ultrasound was non-diagnostic.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate next investigation?
o: CT abdomen and pelvis with contrast
practice.e: In an adult with an unclear diagnosis or equivocal ultrasound, CT with contrast is the imaging of choice and also excludes alternatives such as caecal cancer.

steps.x: Next investigation after a non-diagnostic ultrasound.
Older adult, unclear picture: CT territory.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **CT abdomen and pelvis with contrast**.

elim: AXR does not show appendicitis.
Colonoscopy is dangerous in acute inflammation.
Laparoscopy is invasive; image first when stable.
Repeating a non-diagnostic USS adds little in an adult.

steps.x: **C. CT with contrast.** Adults, unclear or equivocal USS = CT.

practice.stem: A 27 year old man has a 1 day history of migratory right iliac fossa pain, anorexia and fever. Ultrasound shows uncomplicated acute appendicitis with no perforation. His temperature is 37.9°C, pulse rate 102 bpm and BP 122/76 mmHg. He has been given IV fluids, analgesia and prophylactic IV antibiotics.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate definitive management?
practice.e: Early laparoscopic appendicectomy is the definitive treatment for acute appendicitis. Interval surgery is for an appendix mass that has not settled.

steps.x: Definitive management of uncomplicated appendicitis.
First-line steps done; no mass, no perforation.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Early laparoscopic appendicectomy**.

elim: Interval surgery is for an appendix mass.
Discharge on oral antibiotics is unsafe here.
Drainage is for an abscess.
Hemicolectomy is for caecal cancer or large carcinoids.

steps.x: **B. Laparoscopic appendicectomy.**

practice.stem: A 36 year old woman presents after 8 days of right iliac fossa pain. She has a tender mass in the right iliac fossa and a swinging fever. Ultrasound shows a 5 cm collection next to the caecum. Her temperature is 38.6°C, pulse rate 104 bpm and BP 118/74 mmHg. Her abdomen is soft elsewhere.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
o: IV antibiotics and drainage of the collection
practice.e: An appendix mass with abscess is treated with IV antibiotics and drainage, with delayed (interval) surgery. Immediate surgery into an inflamed mass risks damaging the bowel.

steps.x: Initial management of a complication.

clues: tender mass in the right iliac fossa
steps.x: Late presentation, walled-off abscess, no generalised peritonitis.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **IV antibiotics and drainage**, then interval surgery.

elim: No generalised peritonitis, so no laparotomy.
Operating on an inflamed mass risks bowel injury.
She is febrile with an abscess.
No suggestion of malignancy.

steps.x: **B. IV antibiotics and drainage.** Interval appendicectomy if not settled at 6 weeks.

practice.stem: A 19 year old man with acute appendicitis is listed for laparoscopic appendicectomy. He has no drug allergies. His temperature is 37.8°C, pulse rate 98 bpm and BP 126/80 mmHg. The surgeon asks for his antibiotics to be prescribed.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate antibiotic regimen?
practice.e: IV amoxicillin, gentamicin and metronidazole cover gut Gram-positives, Gram-negatives and anaerobes, given one dose before and two doses after surgery.

steps.x: Antibiotic choice for appendicectomy.
Gut flora: need Gram-negative and anaerobic cover.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **IV amoxicillin, gentamicin, metronidazole**.

elim: No Gram-negative or anaerobic cover.
Vancomycin covers Gram-positives only.
Oral macrolide is for atypical chest infection.
Nitrofurantoin is for lower UTI.

steps.x: **A. Amoxicillin, gentamicin and metronidazole.** One dose before, two after, for 24 hours.

practice.stem: A 22 year old woman describes her appendicitis pain as starting as a vague ache around her umbilicus before moving to the right iliac fossa 12 hours later. Her temperature is 37.8°C and pulse rate 98 bpm.
practice.q: Which is the most likely explanation for the initial periumbilical pain?
o: Referred visceral pain via midgut autonomic afferents
practice.e: Distension of the midgut-derived appendix gives poorly localised visceral pain referred to the periumbilical region. Parietal peritoneal irritation causes the later, localised RIF pain.

steps.x: Mechanism of the first phase of pain.

clues: moving to the right iliac fossa 12 hours later
steps.x: Vague and central = visceral; sharp and localised later = somatic.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Visceral pain referred via midgut autonomic nerves.**

elim: Obturator irritation is a pelvic appendix sign.
Parietal irritation explains the later RIF pain.
Phrenic irritation refers to the shoulder tip.
Not a recognised mechanism of appendiceal pain.

steps.x: **D. Referred visceral pain.** Midgut = periumbilical.

UTI or ureteric colic: urine dip abnormal, loin pain

prompts.tip: Exam thinking: who is the patient decides the scan.

prompts.q: How do you manage uncomplicated acute appendicitis?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: definitive means the operation.

Prophylactic IV antibiotics before surgery

prompts.tip: Exam thinking: veins fail before arteries.

glossary.appendicitis: Inflammation of the appendix, usually from blockage of its lumen.
glossary.faecolith: A hard lump of stool that can block the appendix lumen.
glossary.lymphoid hyperplasia: Swelling of lymphoid tissue in the appendix wall, often after a viral illness.
glossary.lumen: The hollow inside of a tube-shaped organ.
glossary.RIF: Right iliac fossa: the lower right area of the abdomen.
glossary.LIF: Left iliac fossa: the lower left area of the abdomen.
glossary.McBurney's point: One-third of the way from the right ASIS to the umbilicus; the classic point of appendix tenderness.
glossary.ASIS: Anterior superior iliac spine, the bony point at the front of the hip.
glossary.Rovsing's sign: Pain in the right iliac fossa when the left iliac fossa is pressed.
glossary.psoas sign: Pain on hyperextension of the right hip, suggesting a retrocaecal appendix.
glossary.obturator sign: Pain on internal rotation of the flexed right hip, suggesting a pelvic appendix.
glossary.caecum: The first pouch of the large bowel, where the appendix attaches.
glossary.guarding: Involuntary tensing of the abdominal muscles when pressed, a sign of peritonism.
glossary.rebound tenderness: Pain when pressure on the abdomen is suddenly released, a sign of peritoneal irritation.
glossary.peritonitis: Inflammation of the peritoneum lining the abdomen, giving a rigid, very tender abdomen.
glossary.parietal peritoneum: The peritoneum lining the abdominal wall; it has somatic nerves, so pain is well localised.
glossary.visceral pain: Dull, poorly localised pain from stretched or inflamed organs, felt in the midline.
glossary.somatic pain: Sharp, well-localised pain from the body wall or parietal peritoneum.
glossary.midgut: Embryological gut from the duodenum to two-thirds along the transverse colon; its pain is felt periumbilically.
glossary.appendix mass: An inflamed appendix walled off by omentum and bowel, felt as a tender RIF lump.
glossary.appendicular abscess: A pus collection around the appendix, often after perforation, causing swinging fever.
glossary.interval appendicectomy: Removal of the appendix weeks after an appendix mass or abscess has settled.
glossary.swinging fever: A temperature that rises and falls repeatedly, typical of an abscess.
glossary.omentum: A fatty apron hanging from the stomach that can wall off infection.
glossary.beta-hCG: Pregnancy hormone; measured to exclude ectopic pregnancy.
glossary.ectopic pregnancy: A pregnancy outside the uterus, usually in a fallopian tube.
glossary.laparoscopic: Keyhole surgery through small incisions with a camera.
glossary.mesenteric adenitis: Inflamed abdominal lymph nodes after a viral illness, mimicking appendicitis.
glossary.NBM: Nil by mouth: nothing to eat or drink.
glossary.histology: Examination of tissue under a microscope.
glossary.gentamicin: An IV aminoglycoside antibiotic covering Gram-negative bacteria.
glossary.CRP: C-reactive protein, a blood marker of inflammation.
